rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Fatiha is Umm al-Qur'an because it opens the Qur'an and is like its root and origin, hence al-Asās.
rows.anchor: وتسمى أم القرآن ،   لأنها مفتتحه ومبدؤه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It is also Umm al-Qur'an because it gathers praise, worship of commands and prohibitions, promise and threat, theoretical wisdom, practical guidance, and knowledge of the blessed and wretched.
rows.anchor: أو لأنها تشتمل على ما فيه من الثناء على الله سبحانه وتعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Its other names include al-Kanz, al-Wāfiya, al-Kāfiya, al-Ḥamd, al-Shukr, al-Duʿāʾ, Taʿlīm al-Masʾala, and al-Ṣalāt; the latter names reflect its supplication and prayer recitation.
rows.anchor: وسورة الكنز والوافية والكافية لذلك

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet is quoted saying al-Fatiha is a cure for every illness, explaining its names al-Shāfiya and al-Shifāʾ.
rows.anchor: والشافية والشفاء لقوله عليه الصلاة والسلام :  " هي شفاء من كل داء "

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It is called the Seven Oft-Repeated because it comprises seven verses by agreement.
rows.anchor: والسبع المثاني لأنها سبع آيات بالاتفاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One group counts the basmala but not “those upon whom You bestowed favor” as a verse.
rows.anchor: منهم من عد التسمية دون { أنعمت عليهم }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another group excludes the basmala and counts “those upon whom You bestowed favor.”
rows.anchor: ومنهم من عكس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It is repeated in prayer, or—if the report is sound—was revealed in Mecca when prayer was imposed and in Medina when the qibla changed.
rows.anchor: وتثنى في الصلاة ،   أو الإنزال إن صح أنها نزلت بمكة حين فرضت الصلاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bayḍāwī confirms it is Meccan, citing the Meccan verse that says God gave the Prophet the seven oft-repeated verses.
rows.anchor: وقد صح أنها مكية لقوله تعالى { ولقد آتيناك سبعا من المثاني }

rows.speaker: قراء مكة والكوفة وفقهاؤهما وابن المبارك والشافعي
rows.claim: Meccan and Kufan reciters and jurists, Ibn al-Mubārak, and al-Shāfiʿī hold that the basmala is part of al-Fatiha and every sūra.
rows.anchor: وعليه قراء مكة والكوفة وفقهاؤهما وابن المبارك رحمه الله تعالى والشافعي

rows.speaker: قراء المدينة والبصرة والشام وفقهاؤها ومالك والأوزاعي
rows.claim: The reciters and jurists of Medina, Basra, and Syria, Mālik, and al-Awzāʿī reject its being part of every sūra.
rows.anchor: خالفهم قراء المدينة والبصرة والشام وفقهاؤها ومالك والأوزاعي

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abū Ḥanīfa gave no explicit ruling here; Bayḍāwī infers that he considered the basmala outside the sūra.
rows.anchor: ولم ينص أبو حنيفة رحمه الله تعالى فيه بشيء فظن أنها ليست من السورة عنده

rows.speaker: محمد بن الحسن
rows.claim: Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan said that everything between the two covers is God's speech.
rows.anchor: وسئل محمد بن الحسن عنها فقال : ما بين الدفتين كلام الله تعالى

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: Abū Hurayra reports the Prophet saying al-Fatiha has seven verses and its first is the basmala.
rows.anchor: روى أبو هريرة رضي الله تعالى عنه ،   أنه عليه الصلاة والسلام قال

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: Umm Salama reports the Prophet counted the basmala and “Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds” as one verse.
rows.anchor: وقول أم سلمة رضي الله عنها  " قرأ رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم الفاتحة وعد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reports explain the disagreement whether the basmala is a separate verse or part of the following verse.
rows.anchor: ومن أجلهما اختلف في أنها آية برأسها أم بما بعدها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: There is consensus that the muṣḥaf text is God's speech and agreement to include the basmala in muṣḥafs despite rigorous exclusion of non-Qur'anic matter.
rows.anchor: والإجماع على أن ما بين الدفتين كلام الله سبحانه وتعالى ،   والوفاق على إثباتها في المصاحف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bāʾ attaches to omitted “I read,” since what follows is recited; this is better than “I begin,” unsupported by context, or “my beginning,” requiring extra ellipsis.
rows.anchor: والباء متعلقة بمحذوف تقديره : بسم الله أقرأ لأن الذي يتلوه مقروء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fronting the phrase emphasizes exclusivity and reverence, accords with God's name preceding recitation, and makes it the instrument of an act not ritually complete without it.
rows.anchor: وتقديم المعمول ههنا أوقع كما في قوله : { بسم الله مجراها } وقوله { إياك نعبد }

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet is quoted saying every important matter not begun with the basmala is deficient.
rows.anchor: لقوله عليه الصلاة والسلام  " كل أمر ذي بال لا يبدأ فيه ببسم الله فهو أبتر "

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, bāʾ denotes accompaniment: “I read while blessed by God's name.”
rows.anchor: وقيل الباء للمصاحبة ،   والمعنى متبركا باسم الله تعالى اقرأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The basmala and rest of the sūra are put on servants' tongues to teach invocation for blessing, praise of God's favors, and asking His bounty.
rows.anchor: وهذه وما بعده إلى آخر السورة مقول على ألسنة العباد ليعلموا كيف يتبرك باسمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bāʾ is kasra as a bound genitive preposition; command and possessive lām are likewise kasra before nouns to distinguish them from lām of inception.
rows.anchor: وإنما كسرت ومن حق الحروف المفردة أن تفتح

rows.speaker: أصحابنا البصريون
rows.claim: Basran grammarians derive ism from a form whose ending was dropped for frequent use; hamzat al-waṣl allows its consonant-initial form to begin a word.
rows.anchor: والاسم عند أصحابنا البصريين من الأسماء التي حذفت أعجازها لكثرة الاستعمال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Forms asmāʾ, asāmī, samā, and samīt support this derivation; poetry attests the form samy.
rows.anchor: ويشهد له تصريفه على أسماء وأسامي وسمى وسميت ومجيء سمى كهدى لغة فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bayḍāwī rejects metathesis as irregular and derives ism from sumūw, elevation, since a name raises and marks its referent.
rows.anchor: والقلب بعيد غير مطرد ،   واشتقاقه من السمو لأنه رفعة للمسمى وشعار له

rows.speaker: الكوفيون
rows.claim: The Kufans derive ism from sima, “mark”: its original was wasm, with initial wāw deleted and hamzat al-waṣl added to reduce irregularity.
rows.anchor: ومن السمة عند الكوفيين ،   وأصله وسم حذفت الواو وعوضت عنها همزة الوصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bayḍāwī objects that Arabic has no precedent for hamza entering a word after its first letter has been deleted.
rows.anchor: ورد بأن الهمزة لم تعهد داخلة على ما حذف صدره في كلامهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sam and sim are also forms; a poem attests sam in the phrase “in the name of the one in every sūra.”
rows.anchor: ومن لغاته سم وسم قال : بسم الذي في كل سورة سمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If ism means the spoken word, it differs from its referent: transient sounds vary across peoples and eras and may be multiple or singular, unlike the named entity.
rows.anchor: والاسم إن أريد به اللفظ فغير المسمى ،   لأنه يتألف من أصوات متقطعة غير قارة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If ism means the entity itself, it is the named thing, though this sense is not established in common usage.
rows.anchor: وإن أريد به ذات الشيء فهو المسمى لكنه لم يشتهر بهذا المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Qur'anic commands to glorify God's name, “name” means the word: as God's essence and attributes must be kept from defects, so must their names from obscenity and discourtesy.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى : { تبارك اسم ربك } و{ سبح اسم ربك } المراد به اللفظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “name” is an insertion without independent meaning, as in the poet's line “then the name of peace be upon you both.”
rows.anchor: أو الاسم فيه مقحم كما في قول الشاعر : إلى الحول ثم اسم السلام عليكما

rows.speaker: أبو الحسن الأشعري
rows.claim: Al-Ashʿarī regards a name as an attribute, which divides into what is the same as the named, other than it, or neither same nor other.
rows.anchor: كما هو رأي الشيخ أبي الحسن الأشعري ،   انقسم انقسام الصفة عنده : إلى ما هو نفس المسمى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “In God's name” rather than “by God” invokes blessing and aid through mention of His name, or distinguishes seeking blessing from swearing.
rows.anchor: وإنما قال بسم الله ولم يقل بالله ،   لأن التبرك والاستعانة بذكر اسمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The written alif is omitted by orthographic convention due to frequency, and the bāʾ is lengthened in compensation.
rows.anchor: ولم تكتب الألف على ما هو وضع الخط لكثرة الاستعمال وطولت الباء عوضا عنها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Allāh is said to derive from ilāh, with hamza deleted and replaced by the article; ilāh originally meant any deity but came to designate the true deity.
rows.anchor: والله أصله إله ،   فحذفت الهمزة وعوض عنها الألف واللام ولذلك قيل : يا الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Proposed roots of ilāh include worship, bewilderment, and finding rest with someone, since hearts find tranquility in God's remembrance.
rows.anchor: واشتقاقه من أله ألهة وألوهة وألوهية بمعنى عبد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other proposals compare worshippers' clinging in hardship to a calf clinging to its mother, or derive the word from fleeing in fear and receiving refuge.
rows.anchor: أو من أله إذا فزع من أمر نزل عليه ،   وآلهة غيره أجاره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further proposal derives it from walaha, bewilderment, with wāw changed to hamza under kasra; Bayḍāwī objects that its plural is āliha, not awliha.
rows.anchor: وكان أصله ولاه فقلبت الواو همزة لاستثقال الكسرة عليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another derivation takes it from lāh, hidden and elevated: God is beyond sight and above all things; a cited poem uses lāh.
rows.anchor: وقيل أصله لاه مصدر لاه يليه ليها ولاها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view makes Allāh the unique proper name: it is described but not itself descriptive and uniquely names the one whose attributes are predicated.
rows.anchor: وقيل علم لذاته المخصوصة لأنه يوصف ولا يوصف به ،   ولأنه لا بد له من اسم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: That view argues that a merely descriptive reading would not make “no deity but God” a statement of unity or exclude partnership.
rows.anchor: ولأنه لو كان وصفا لم يكن قول : لا إله إلا الله ،   توحيدا مثل : لا إله إلا الرحمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bayḍāwī prefers that Allāh was originally descriptive but became name-like through exclusive use, allowing predicates while excluding descriptive use and partners.
rows.anchor: والأظهر أنه وصف في أصله لكنه لما غلب عليه بحيث لا يستعمل في غيره وصار له كالعلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unqualified essence is unknowable to humans and cannot be named; a merely proper-name reading also fails to explain “He is God in the heavens.”
rows.anchor: لأن ذاته من حيث هو بلا اعتبار أمر آخر حقيقي أو غيره غير معقول للبشر ،   فلا يمكن أن يدل عليه بلفظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another proposal derives the word from Syriac lāhā, arabized by dropping the final alif and adding lām.
rows.anchor: وقيل أصله لاها بالسريانية فعرب بحذف الألف الأخيرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām is traditionally velarized after fatḥa or ḍamma; some say it is always velarized.
rows.anchor: وتفخيم لامه إذا انفتح ما قبله أو انضم سنة ،   وقيل مطلقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Deleting Allāh's alif is an error that invalidates prayer and does not establish an explicit oath, though poetic necessity may require it.
rows.anchor: وحذف ألفه لحن تفسد به الصلاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm are intensive forms from raḥima, like ghaḍbān from ghaḍiba and ʿalīm from ʿalima.
rows.anchor: اسمان بنيا للمبالغة من رحم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mercy linguistically is tenderness of heart and an inclination entailing benefaction; a womb is named raḥim because it inclines over what it contains.
rows.anchor: والرحمة في اللغة : رقة القلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Divine names are understood by resultant acts and ends, not by the passive beginnings of human mercy.
rows.anchor: وأسماء الله تعالى إنما تؤخذ باعتبار الغايات التي هي أفعال دون المبادي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Raḥmān is more emphatic than al-Raḥīm because the expanded form indicates greater meaning by quantity or quality.
rows.anchor: و{ الرحمن } أبلغ من { الرحيم } ،   لأن زيادة البناء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By quantity, al-Raḥmān is worldly mercy shared by believers and unbelievers, while al-Raḥīm is afterlife mercy for believers.
rows.anchor: فعلى الأول قيل : يا رحمن الدنيا لأنه يعم المؤمن والكافر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By quality, al-Raḥmān denotes mercy in both worlds and al-Raḥīm mercy in this world, since afterlife blessings are immense and worldly ones vary in size.
rows.anchor: وعلى الثاني قيل : يا رحمن الدنيا والآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though rhetoric might progress from lesser to greater, al-Raḥmān comes first because worldly mercy precedes the afterlife.
rows.anchor: وإنما قدم والقياس يقتضي الترقي من الأدنى إلى الأعلى ،   لتقدم رحمة الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Raḥmān precedes as God's exclusive name, the true ultimate benefactor; others give from mixed motives and only mediate blessings God creates and enables.
rows.anchor: ولأنه صار كالعلم من حيث إنه لا يوصف به غيره لأن معناه المنعم الحقيقي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, al-Raḥmān denotes great blessings and al-Raḥīm completes it by including blessings outside that category.
rows.anchor: أو لأن الرحمن لما دل على جلائل النعم وأوصلها ذكر الرحيم ليتناول ما خرج منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The order may also preserve the sūra's verse-end rhyme.
rows.anchor: أو للمحافظة على رؤوس الآي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bayḍāwī's preferred analysis leaves al-Raḥmān diptote despite its exclusivity to God, preventing usual feminine forms in this pattern.
rows.anchor: والأظهر أنه غير مصروف وإن حظر اختصاصه بالله تعالى أن يكون له مؤنث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These names teach that only the true deity, master of all near and future blessings great and small, deserves invocation; worshippers should turn wholly to God and rely on His enabling help.
rows.anchor: وإنما خص التسمية بهذه الأسماء ليعلم العارف أن المستحق لأن يستعان به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥamd praises chosen goodness, whether a blessing or otherwise; madh praises goodness without qualification, so one praises knowledge and generosity but only commends beauty.
rows.anchor: الحمد هو الثناء على الجميل الاختياري من نعمة أو غيرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some consider ḥamd and madh synonymous or close companions.
rows.anchor: وقيل هما أخوان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shukr responds to a blessing through speech, action, and belief; a poem names hand, tongue, and hidden heart as the three responses.
rows.anchor: والشكر : مقابلة النعمة قولا وعملا واعتقادا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shukr is broader than ḥamd and madh in one respect and narrower in another; praise is a branch of gratitude and better signals blessings than hidden belief or ambiguous bodily acts, so it is gratitude's chief element.
rows.anchor: ولما كان الحمد من شعب الشكر أشيع للنعمة ،   وأدل على مكانها

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet is quoted saying praise is the head of gratitude and that whoever does not praise God has not thanked Him.
rows.anchor: فقال عليه الصلاة والسلام :  " الحمد رأس الشكر ،   وما شكر الله من لم يحمده "

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Blame is the opposite of praise, and ingratitude the opposite of shukr.
rows.anchor: والذم نقيض الحمد والكفران نقيض الشكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ḥamdu is nominative as subject with “to God” as predicate, though an accusative reading is also reported.
rows.anchor: ورفعه بالابتداء وخبره لله وأصله النصب وقد قرئ به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nominative conveys universal and permanent praise belonging to God rather than newly arising praise.
rows.anchor: وإنما عدل عنه إلى الرفع ليدل على عموم الحمد وثباته له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥamd is a verbal noun normally governed by an implicit, rarely used verb; its article may denote the genus or point to the familiar idea of praise.
rows.anchor: وهو من المصادر التي تنصب بأفعال مضمرة لا تكاد تستعمل معها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the article is exhaustive, all praise belongs to God because He bestows every good directly or indirectly; this implies He is living, powerful, willing, and knowing.
rows.anchor: إذ الحمد في الحقيقة كله له ،   إذ ما من خير إلا وهو موليه بوسط أو بغير وسط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readings assimilate dāl and lām in opposite directions, treating the letters as one word because they are used together.
rows.anchor: وقرئ الحمد لله بإتباع الدال اللام وبالعكس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rabb originally means tarbiya, bringing something to perfection little by little, then became an intensive description like ṣawm and ʿadl.
rows.anchor: الرب في الأصل مصدر بمعنى التربية : وهي تبليغ الشيء إلى كماله شيئا فشيئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another derivation makes rabb a descriptive form from rabba-yarubbuhu; it then means owner because an owner preserves and nurtures what is owned.
rows.anchor: وقيل هو نعت من ربه يربه فهو رب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rabb is unqualified for God alone, though it can be qualified for others, as in “return to your lord.”
rows.anchor: ولا يطلق على غيره تعالى إلا مقيدا كقوله { ارجع إلى ربك }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿĀlam means what makes something known, like a signet or mold; it came to denote all besides God, substances and accidents, whose contingency indicates the necessary Creator.
rows.anchor: والعالم اسم لما يعلم به ،   كالخاتم والقالب ،   غلب فيما يعلم به الصانع تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural encompasses diverse classes and uses the masculine rational plural because rational beings predominate among them.
rows.anchor: وإنما جمعه ليشمل ما تحته من الأجناس المختلفة ،   وغلب العقلاء منهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view restricts al-ʿālamīn to rational beings—angels and the human and jinn races—with others included secondarily.
rows.anchor: وقيل اسم وضع لذوي العلم من الملائكة والثقلين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further view takes it here to mean people: each person contains counterparts of the cosmos that reveal the Creator, as in the verse about looking within oneself.
rows.anchor: وقيل عني به الناس ههنا فإن كل واحد منهم عالم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusative rabb al-ʿālamīn is analyzed as praise, a vocative, or an implied verb indicated by “praise.”
rows.anchor: وقرئ { رب العالمين } بالنصب على المدح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Contingent things need an originator at coming-to-be and a sustainer for as long as they exist.
rows.anchor: وفيه دليل على أن الممكنات كما هي مفتقرة إلى المحدث حال حدوثها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated “al-Raḥmān, al-Raḥīm” supplies a causal explanation, which Bayḍāwī will discuss below.
rows.anchor: كرره للتعليل على ما سنذكره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After naming the one deserving praise and describing His distinguishing attributes, the discourse directly addresses Him; this moves from proof and absence to presence and witnessing, the knower's culmination after reflection on God's names, gifts, and works.
rows.anchor: ثم إنه لما ذكر الحقيق بالحمد ،   ووصف بصفات عظام تميز بها عن سائر الذوات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabs vary person and address to refresh speech and engage listeners; Bayḍāwī illustrates the shift with Qur'anic examples and Imruʾ al-Qays's changing pronouns.
rows.anchor: ومن عادة العرب التفنن في الكلام والعدول من أسلوب إلى آخر تطرية له وتنشيطا للسامع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iyyā is a detached accusative pronoun; attached yāʾ, kāf, or hāʾ marks person and has no syntactic position, like tāʾ in anta and kāf in araʾaytaka.
rows.anchor: وإيا ضمير منصوب منفصل ،   وما يلحقه من الياء والكاف والهاء حروف زيدت لبيان

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl analyzes iyyā as a noun to which attached pronouns are genitive, citing an Arab saying about a man reaching sixty and young women.
rows.anchor: وقال الخليل إيا مضاف إليها ،   واحتج بما حكاه عن بعض العرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bayḍāwī dismisses al-Khalīl's evidence as anomalous and unreliable.
rows.anchor: وهو شاذ لا يعتمد عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One analysis makes suffixes the pronouns and iyyā their support because pronouns detached from governors cannot be pronounced alone.
rows.anchor: وقيل هي الضمائر ،   وإيا عمدة فإنها لما فصلت عن العوامل تعذر النطق بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another analysis treats the whole form—iyyā plus suffix—as the pronoun.
rows.anchor: وقيل : الضمير هو المجموع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reported readings include iyyāka with fatḥa on hamza and hiyyāka with hamza changed to hāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرئ { إياك } بفتح الهمزة و " هياك "

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿIbāda is utmost submission and humility, from maʿbad, a smoothed road, and a garment of exceptional thickness; thus it is used only for submission to God.
rows.anchor: والعبادة : أقصى غاية الخضوع والتذلل ومنه طريق معبد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Istiʿāna is seeking help. Necessary assistance includes capacity, conceiving the act, tools, and material; when these obtain, one can be morally commanded.
rows.anchor: طلب المعونة وهي : إما ضرورية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nonessential help makes an act easier or motivates it, like a mount for one able to walk; it is not required for valid moral responsibility.
rows.anchor: وغير الضرورية تحصيل ما يتيسر به الفعل ويسهل كالراحلة في السفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The request may concern every important matter or specifically performance of worship.
rows.anchor: والمراد طلب المعونة في المهمات كلها ،   أو في أداء العبادات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The implicit “we” may include reciter, guardian angels, and those at congregational prayer, or all monotheists; sharing their worship and need seeks acceptance through their blessing and explains communal prayer.
rows.anchor: والضمير المستكن في الفعلين للقارئ ومن معه من الحفظة ،   وحاضري صلاة الجماعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fronting the object signals reverence, importance, and exclusivity; Ibn ʿAbbās glosses it “We worship You and no other.”
rows.anchor: ولذلك قال ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما ( معناه نعبدك ولا نعبد غيرك )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The worshipper attends first to God and views worship as a noble relation, not personal achievement; the gnostic reaches communion through total attention to God and loss of self-awareness.
rows.anchor: ومنه إلى العبادة لا من حيث إنها عبادة صدرت عنه بل من حيث إنها نسبة شريفة إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bayḍāwī prefers the beloved Prophet's “Do not grieve; God is with us” to Moses's “My Lord is with me and will guide me,” because the first foregrounds God's presence.
rows.anchor: ولذلك فضل ما حكى الله عن حبيبه حين قال { لا تحزن إن الله معنا } على ما حكاه عن كليمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating iyyāka makes explicit that God alone is sought for help.
rows.anchor: وكرر الضمير للتنصيص على أنه المستعان به لا غير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worship comes first to preserve verse endings and because presenting the means before requesting a need makes a response more likely.
rows.anchor: ويعلم منه أن تقديم الوسيلة على طلب الحاجة أدعى إلى الإجابة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ascribing worship to oneself might imply pride, so the following request shows worship cannot occur or endure without God's aid and enabling grace.
rows.anchor: وأقول : لما نسب المتكلم العبادة إلى نفسه أوهم ذلك تبجحا واعتدادا منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another analysis takes the conjunction as circumstantial: “We worship You while seeking Your help.”
rows.anchor: وقيل : الواو للحال والمعنى نعبدك مستعينين بك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kasra on both nūns follows Tamim dialect, which kasras imperfect prefixes other than yāʾ if the following vowel is not ḍamma.
rows.anchor: وقرئ بكسر النون فيهما وهي لغة بني تميم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Guide us” explains the requested assistance—as if God asked how to help—or singles out its greatest aim.
rows.anchor: بيان للمعونة المطلوبة فكأنه قال : كيف أعينكم فقالوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hidāya is gentle direction, normally used for good; “lead them to Hell's path” is sarcastic. Related hawādī are the foreparts that lead wild animals.
rows.anchor: والهداية دلالة بلطف ولذلك تستعمل في الخير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hadā normally governs li- or ilā but here is treated like ikhtāra in “Moses chose his people.”
rows.anchor: والفعل منه هدى ،   وأصله أن يعدى باللام ،   أو إلى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's kinds of guidance are innumerable like His blessings, yet can be classified in an ordered scheme.
rows.anchor: وهداية الله تعالى تتنوع أنواعا لا يحصيها عد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first kind grants capacities for finding one's interests, including reason, inner senses, and external perception.
rows.anchor: الأول : إفاضة القوى التي بها يتمكن المرء من الاهتداء إلى مصالحه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second kind presents signs distinguishing truth from falsehood and good from corruption; verses say people were shown the two paths and Thamud chose blindness.
rows.anchor: نصب الدلائل الفارقة بين الحق والباطل والصلاح والفساد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The third kind guides through messengers and revealed books, exemplified by leaders guiding by God's command and the Qur'an guiding to the upright path.
rows.anchor: الهداية بإرسال الرسل وإنزال الكتب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fourth kind unveils realities to hearts through revelation, inspiration, or true dreams; only prophets and saints attain it.
rows.anchor: الرابع أن يكشف على قلوبهم السرائر ويريهم الأشياء كما هي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The request may seek increased guidance, perseverance in it, or higher ranks built upon it.
rows.anchor: فالمطلوب إما زيادة ما منحوه من الهدى ،   أو الثبات عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A gnostic who has reached God seeks guidance along the journey to Him, removal of spiritual darkness and bodily veils, and vision by God's holy light.
rows.anchor: فإذا قاله العارف بالله الواصل عنى به أرشدنا طريق السير فيك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Command and supplication share wording and meaning but differ by superiority or inferiority; another view says the difference is rank.
rows.anchor: والأمر والدعاء يتشاركان لفظا ومعنى ويتفاوتان بالاستعلاء والتسفل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣirāṭ is linked to sarata, swallowing: the road seems to swallow travelers, hence the name luqam, “gulper.”
rows.anchor: والسراط : من سرط الطعام إذا ابتلعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣād replaces original sīn to match emphatic ṭāʾ; the ṣād may be colored with zāy to approach the replaced letter.
rows.anchor: و{ الصراط } من قلب السين صادا ليطابق الطاء في الإطباق

rows.speaker: ابن كثير برواية قنبل ورويس عن يعقوب
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr through Qunbul and Ruways from Yaʿqūb read original sīn; Ḥamza uses the mixed pronunciation and others read ṣād, the Quraysh dialect.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير برواية قنبل عنه ،   ورويس عن يعقوب بالأصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣirāṭ's plural is suruṭ, like kutub; like ṭarīq, it may be masculine or feminine.
rows.anchor: والثابت في الإمام وجمعه سرط ككتب وهو كالطريق في التذكير والتأنيث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-mustaqīm means level or straight; its intended referent is the path of truth.
rows.anchor: المستوي والمراد به طريق الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative identifies the straight path as the religion of Islam.
rows.anchor: وقيل هو ملة الإسلام
